title: Show HN: Git blame for AI code, down to the agent session
content:
git blame for agent sessions
Point at a line your agent wrote. Read the session that wrote it.
git blame stops at a commit and a name, usually yours. KeepPlain follows the line to the Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi or Antigravity session behind it and opens the turn: what you asked, what the agent tried first, why it changed.
curl -fsSL https://keepplain.com/install.sh | sh    # macOS and Linux
irm https://keepplain.com/install.ps1 | iex         # Windows, in PowerShell
keepplain login
keepplain enable
Free for personal use. Say yes when keepplain enable asks about git hooks: they add the session’s id to your commits, and blame follows it.
On Windows you can also get it from the Microsoft Store.
Git says who changed it. It can’t say why.
Ask your agent about a line, and it follows git to the session that made the change, reads the turns from your request to the commit, and answers with quotes. It says which turns it read and how the session was found.
> why is line 42 of src/auth/login.ts keyed by account?
Deliberate. On Sep 30 the agent first keyed the limit by IP, and 2 of 41
tests failed: behind the load balancer every user shares one address.
You said:
  “Behind the load balancer everyone has the same IP. Key it by the account.”
It switched the key to the email being signed in to and committed a3f9e1c.
quoted from turns 112–115 of your Claude Code session
What your agent answers, in any of the five agents.
Ask in plain words. No new command to learn.
When a prompt asks where code came from, the plugin adds one line to it: git shows what changed, the session the change was made in shows why. So the agent runs git log or git blame first, then asks KeepPlain for the session by the commit, its trailer, its subject and the files. The match is made on your computer; the prompt goes nowhere.
> why is line 42 of src/auth/login.ts keyed by account?
> where did the retry loop in sync.ts come from?
> why was commit e93b2aa made?
> who added the lock in syncSeats, and why?
> откуда взялся этот таймаут?
Things people type. English and Russian both work.
On the site, a link to a line gives its whole life.
git blame shows the last commit. In your team’s search, a GitHub link ending in #L42 becomes the line’s history: the commit that added it, every commit that changed it, and the sessions behind each one.
https://github.com/acme/api/blob/main/src/auth/login.ts#L42
On the pull request, for teams.
Switch it on for your team and the GitHub App keeps one comment on each pull request, updated as commits change: which commits came from a session, which were agent-assisted, and the session behind each.
- Off until a team owner turns it on.
- Session titles only in private repositories. In a public one the link opens the team’s page, for members.
- No prompt, no text, no file in the comment.
keepplain bot · commented, edited 2 min ago
Sessions behind this pull request. The commits that came from an agent session or with an agent’s help.
From KeepPlain, for the Acme team: the sessions open there for the team. Owners and admins turn this comment off in the team’s settings.
How it follows a line
No new version control and no IDE extension. The agent you already use runs git, then asks KeepPlain.
- The line’s whole history git blame names only the last commit. Your agent asks git for every commit that touched the line, up to eight.
$ git log -L 42,42:src/auth/login.ts -s --date=short \
    --format='%h  %ad  %s  %(trailers:key=Agent-Session,valueonly)'
a3f9e1c  2026-09-30  Key login rate limit by account   7c21e0b4-…
6d12f9a  2026-09-15  Tighten login limit
1b07c44  2026-09-02  Add login throttle                91e5aa20-… Three commits touched line 42. Two of them name the session they came from.
- The commit names its session One trailer line in the commit message, written by KeepPlain’s prepare-commit-msg hook when a commit holds a session’s work. Only the id travels with your push. The session doesn’t.
$ git show -s --format=%B a3f9e1c Key login rate limit by account Agent-Session: 7c21e0b4-2f6e-4a1d-9c3b-58e0f1d2a7b9
- KeepPlain finds the session By the commit, the trailer, the subject and the files, across your sessions from all five agents, and your team’s. search_my_work commit a3f9e1c agent_sessions 7c21e0b4-… subject "Key login rate limit by account" paths src/auth/login.ts → Claude Code · “Rate-limit the login endpoint” · Sep 30 found_by commit own true cursor turn 115 changed src/auth/login.ts, made a3f9e1c request turn 112 “Behind the load balancer everyone has…”
- It reads the turns From your request to the change: the reasoning and your decision, not the whole log. The request is your last real one before the change; a “yes” or “continue” is skipped. get_session_excerpt turns 109–115 109 agent Keying the limiter by IP, the usual default. 110 tests ✕ 2 of 41 failed · users behind one proxy are blocked together 112 you “Behind the load balancer everyone has the same IP. Key it by the account.” 115 agent changed src/auth/login.ts:42 · committed a3f9e1c
- Your agent answers, with quotes The answer above: what happened, your words, the commit, and which turns it came from. If the session was found another way, by its edits or not at all, the answer says that too.
When the trail goes cold, it says so
The answer tells you how the session was found. Or that it wasn’t.
Found by its commit
The commit says which session it came from. The answer quotes that session and the turns it read.
Found by its edits
No trailer? KeepPlain takes the agent’s last edits of those files before the commit, and the answer says it was found that way, not by the commit.
A teammate’s session
You get whose session it is and its page. The conversation stays with its author until they share it.
No agent session found
The change wasn’t made in a synced session you can read. Your agent says so instead of inventing a reason.
What leaves your computer
Git runs on your computer and the code stays there.
What the site gets
The file’s path and its commits: hash, the file’s name in each, title, Agent-Session trailer, dates. The newest 300 commits of a file, a hundred a request. Never the code.
What comes back
The sessions you may read. A teammate’s session you see in the team’s list but may not read is named by its author only.
Signed out
A trailer that names a session the site doesn’t hold is looked for on this computer, and nothing of it goes anywhere. Not signed in, that is all you get, with the commits’ titles for the rest.
The git hooks
Only in a repository where you said yes to keepplain enable, never globally. The session id becomes part of the repository’s history: in a public repository everyone sees it. keepplain disable takes the hooks out; trailers already in commits stay.
Options
-L from,to blames those lines, --rev=commit the file as it was there, -w ignores whitespace, --json is for scripts and the desktop app.
Read the code
The plugin is MIT. Its README describes the command, and the table under “What leaves your machine” lists every call.
Measured, not promised
“why” questions answered with the session that made the change
median answer to a “why”
Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi and Antigravity
of past sessions KeepPlain offers to bring in when you install
Measured in production on Oct 14, 2026: 34 questions the founder asked about their own work, 6 of them “why”, across 391 sessions. For 31 of the 34 the right session came first. One person’s history, not a benchmark.
Next time, ask why.

report.summary: KeepPlain extends git blame beyond commits, tracing each line of AI-written code back to the exact agent session, prompt, and turn that produced it.
report.background: git blame has always answered 'who changed this line and when', not 'why'. That gap was tolerable when a human wrote the line and could be asked. It breaks down when Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi or Antigravity wrote it: the reasoning, the failed attempts, the user's course-correction and the final decision all live in a chat session that evaporates once the terminal closes. Teams reviewing AI-heavy pull requests end up reverse-engineering intent from diffs. Existing provenance tooling stops at commit metadata, and IDE extensions only cover their own editor. KeepPlain's approach is deliberately lightweight: a prepare-commit-msg git hook appends an Agent-Session trailer to commits produced during a session, and the session id — never the transcript — travels with the push. The rest of the matching happens locally, which sidesteps the thorny question of shipping proprietary prompts and source code to a third-party server.
key_points: Blame that reaches the conversation: pointing at a line follows git history to the session behind the commit and opens the turns from the user's request to the change, quoting the user's own words and the agent's reasoning rather than paraphrasing them.

Integration is deliberately unglamorous: no new IDE extension or version-control system. A git hook adds an Agent-Session trailer to commits, and the agent you already use runs git log or git blame first, then asks KeepPlain for the matching session locally.

Privacy is scoped tightly. Code never leaves the machine; the service receives file paths and commit metadata (hash, subject, trailer, dates) for the newest 300 commits of a file. A teammate's session is visible as a name but its contents stay with its author until shared.

Honest failure modes: answers state how the session was found — by commit trailer, by the agent's prior edits to those files, or not at all. When no synced session exists, the agent says so instead of hallucinating a rationale.

Team features are opt-in: a GitHub App keeps one sticky comment on each pull request listing which commits were agent-written or agent-assisted and the session behind each. Off by default, titles only in private repos, no prompts or code in the comment.
report.impact: AI coding agents have quietly broken the audit trail that software teams rely on for review, onboarding, incident postmortems and compliance. KeepPlain is an early attempt to restore it without asking developers to change how they work — the value proposition is that 'why is this line like this' becomes answerable years later, even when the author has left. For agent vendors, session provenance could become a competitive checkbox the way diff review did. For developers, the real test is adoption friction: the hook must survive rebases, squash merges and CI, and the trailer convention needs cross-vendor agreement before it means anything across teams. There is also a governance angle — once sessions are linkable, 'the AI wrote it' stops being a defence, and reviews gain the context they currently lack.
report.tools: KeepPlain itself is MIT-licensed and installable via a one-line curl or PowerShell script, plus a Microsoft Store listing on Windows; commands include keepplain blame <file>, with -L, --rev, -w and --json options. The README documents every network call. It supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi and Antigravity. To follow the underlying technique without the product, study git's own git log -L <from>,<to>:<file> and the %(trailers:key=Agent-Session) format placeholder — both are all you need to prototype lineage tracking yourself.
